questions.prompt:
Part (a): Diagonalise \(A=\begin{pmatrix}13&1\\1&13\end{pmatrix}\).
Part (b): Prove that a real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrix has orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues.
questions.answer:
Part (a)
We need to complete the requested calculation or proof.
Method: Apply the stated mathematical method and simplify each step.
The orthonormal eigenvectors \((1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\) and \((1,-1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\) have eigenvalues \(14\) and \(12\). Thus
\[U=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad U^{\mathsf T}AU=\operatorname{diag}(14,12).\]
Final answer: \(A=U\operatorname{diag}(14,12)U^{\mathsf T}\).

Part (b)
We need to complete the requested calculation or proof.
Method: Apply the stated mathematical method and simplify each step.
If \(A\mathbf u=\lambda\mathbf u\), \(A\mathbf v=\mu\mathbf v\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}=A\), then
\[\lambda\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}\mathbf v=(A\mathbf u)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf v=\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}A\mathbf v=\mu\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}\mathbf v.\]
Since \(\lambda\ne\mu\), the inner product is zero.
Final answer: \(\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}\mathbf v=0\).

questions.prompt:
Part (a): Diagonalise \(A=\begin{pmatrix}14&1\\1&14\end{pmatrix}\).
Part (b): Derive the principal-axis form of \(ax^2+2bxy+cy^2\).
questions.answer:
Part (a)
We need to complete the requested calculation or proof.
Method: Apply the stated mathematical method and simplify each step.
The orthonormal eigenvectors \((1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\) and \((1,-1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\) have eigenvalues \(15\) and \(13\). Thus
\[U=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad U^{\mathsf T}AU=\operatorname{diag}(15,13).\]
Final answer: \(A=U\operatorname{diag}(15,13)U^{\mathsf T}\).

Part (b)
We need to complete the requested calculation or proof.
Method: Apply the stated mathematical method and simplify each step.
The symmetric matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\) has an orthogonal diagonalisation \(M=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)U^{\mathsf T}\). With \((x,y)^{\mathsf T}=U(u,v)^{\mathsf T}\),
\[ax^2+2bxy+cy^2=\lambda_1u^2+\lambda_2v^2.\]
Final answer: The principal-axis form is \(\lambda_1u^2+\lambda_2v^2\).

questions.prompt:
Part (a): Diagonalise \(A=\begin{pmatrix}15&1\\1&15\end{pmatrix}\).
Part (b): Prove that a real symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when all its eigenvalues are positive.
questions.answer:
Part (a)
We need to complete the requested calculation or proof.
Method: Apply the stated mathematical method and simplify each step.
The orthonormal eigenvectors \((1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\) and \((1,-1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\) have eigenvalues \(16\) and \(14\). Thus
\[U=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad U^{\mathsf T}AU=\operatorname{diag}(16,14).\]
Final answer: \(A=U\operatorname{diag}(16,14)U^{\mathsf T}\).

Part (b)
We need to complete the requested calculation or proof.
Method: Apply the stated mathematical method and simplify each step.
Write \(A=U\Lambda U^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\mathbf y=U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x\). Then
\[\mathbf x^{\mathsf T}A\mathbf x=\sum_i\lambda_i y_i^2.\]
This is positive for every nonzero \(\mathbf y\) exactly when each \(\lambda_i>0\).
Final answer: \(A\) is positive definite iff every \(\lambda_i>0\).
